claim: A popular crisp potato descends from one pulled off the market as toxic.

start.title: Potato
start.description: Starchy tuber used as a staple food

knots.passage: Exposure to light, physical damage, and age increase glycoalkaloid content within the tuber. Different potato varieties contain different levels of glycoalkaloids. The 'Lenape' variety, released in 1967, was withdrawn in 1970 as it contained high levels of glycoalkaloids.
knots.hatnote: Potatoes are nightshades, and some carry more natural poison than others.

knots.passage: After the Lenape variety was released for commercial production, a potato breeder in Ontario ate some to see if they might be suitable as new potatoes but soon felt nauseated. When the same occurred next time he ate them, he sent a sample to be analysed by a vegetable biochemist, Dr. Ambrose Zitnak of the University of Guelph, who found they contained exceptionally high levels of glycoalkaloids (mainly solanine and chaconine), the natural toxins found in potatoes that help protect them from pests and disease.
knots.hatnote: Bred for perfect crisps, the Lenape went on sale. Then a breeder tasted some.

knots.passage: Lenape was kept for use in breeding and breeders selected for progeny containing high dry matter but rejected those with high glycoalkaloids. Lenape is a parent of chipping varieties including Atlantic, Trent, Belchip and Snowden and a grandparent of several others. A study published in 1998 found that Lenape had the highest dry matter content of chipping varieties released in the USA and concluded that the release of Lenape marked a "major advance in chipping quality" and was particularly responsible for a trend of increased dry matter content in newer varieties.
knots.hatnote: The toxic potato was banned from sale, but not from the breeding plot.

knots.passage: The Atlantic potato is a mid-season potato variety for potato chip manufacturing. It was developed and released by USDA Agricultural Research Service scientists at Beltsville, Maryland, in 1978. The variety is not under plant variety protection. It is a progeny of a cross between 'Wauseon' and 'Lenape'. It is widely grown for chipping directly off the field or with short-term storage. Marketable yields are fairly high.
knots.hatnote: Its best-known child came from US government scientists.

payoff: The Lenape was too toxic to eat, but its crisp-perfect genes live on in Atlantic, a high-yielding mainstay of the chip fryer.
